portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
I declare open this hearing of the Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I'll begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today, and I pay my respects to their elders past and present. I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today. The committee has fixed Thursday 17 December 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with corporate matters outcomes of the infrastructure, transport and regional development portfolio.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is also unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence. The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings.

I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a Department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted.

Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. An officer called to answer a question for the first time should state their full name and the capacity in which they appear.

Before I go to the official welcoming, I'm also going to make a quick statement. I'd like to speak on behalf of the committee in sending our thoughts to our colleague the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines; her family; her team; and her community as she continues to recover in hospital. The attack against Dr Haines on Monday last week was horrific, and I know we have all come back to this place distressed and in shock at what has happened to our colleague and our friend. Dr Haines is much loved as a colleague here, as a strong advocate for her community back in Indi and indeed around the nation as a fierce participant in our democracy. Contributions will be made in the House of Representatives today from 10 am, and the committee will suspend before 10 am to enable senators to attend the first of these statements as a mark of respect for Dr Haines. I note investigations are under way by Victoria Police, the AFP and ASIO, and I ask senators to please be mindful of this during these hearings. I know this committee will follow that. Doctor Haines is known to all of us as a person of integrity and someone who conducts public debate in a robust but respectful manner. As chair, I will be especially taking this spirit on board through our hearings, and I am sure my fellow senators will join me in this.

Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I now call officers from the department in relation to corporate matters and invite questions. Senator McKenzie.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you for those very apt words. Mr Betts, I actually want to go to the allegations of corruption on public infrastructure sites. It's something we've discussed a lot. Previously, you advised that the department had received 63 reports of allegations of unlawful or corrupt behaviour on Commonwealth funded infrastructure projects, including 56 in Victoria. We're now in October. How many new reports of allegations of unlawful and corrupt behaviour has the department received to date?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We're happy to provide that information to you. In fact, we have a summary table, which I believe we can table, which will set this out for all jurisdictions. But the headlines are that, as of now, total allegations is 84 across 20 projects. That constitutes 4.1 per cent of the infrastructure investment program. And, since the last Senate estimates—
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Is that 4.1 per cent by dollar value or by number of projects?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Purely by number.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I don't have it by dollar value, but we could probably calculate that for you. Since the last Senate estimates, my understanding is that there have been 27 new allegations. I want to emphasise, and this will be made clear in the document that we're tabling, that multiple allegations may relate to a single incident, and that will become apparent during the course of investigation by the relevant regulatory authority. Where allegations have been made, our information is that all allegations have been referred to the relevant regulator and/or law enforcement body.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Can we run through them then, Ms Hall. I would like by project, by nature of allegation and by state—I guess project equals state.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Would you like us to go through the ones that are new since last—
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Let's just get our whole list so there's no confusion.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We can table the list for you.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Would you like us to—
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I would like you to do that, because, if I had the list, I wouldn't have to ask the question, and then I'm going to have to read the list. You've got the list; table the list. But I would like you to run through the list, please.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We have North East Link. There are 19 new allegations since the last estimates. These include allegations overall of fraud, corruption, criminal behaviour, breach of workplace laws, workplace health and safety and undisclosed conflicts of interest. We have SRL East with four since the last estimates. Again, they are allegations of fraud, bullying, corruption, breaches of workplace laws, criminal behaviour and undisclosed conflicts of interest. Then in Victoria there are two that have no specific projects identified; they just go to the Big Build more broadly. Then in—
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The two that go to the Big Build more broadly relate specifically to what?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We don't know which projects they relate to at this stage.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What is the nature of the allegation?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's fraud. Then we have one in South Australia, which is the North-South Corridor, Torrens to Darlington, which is allegations relating to a civil case. Then we have one in New South Wales. The New South Wales government has requested that the project name be withheld, as its disclosure at this time may prejudice an investigation of a possible breach of law. That's in regard to an allegation of corruption.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'll come back to that. New South Wales has one project of an undisclosed nature because it relates to corruption and may undermine the investigation.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's all of the new allegations.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's on top of our original 63.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It would have been 84 minus 27.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: As I understand it, there were two projects where undisclosed conflicts of interest were alleged.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Where was the nature of the undisclosed conflict of interest—the procurement, the subcontractors, the ministers, the public servants? Where was that undisclosed conflict of interest? As I would understand it, it would be odd for a subcontractor working for a tier 1 to be declaring conflicts of interest to come to your attention. Where was the undisclosed conflict of interest raised?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not sure we've got that level of detail for you, because it goes to the information that's provided. I'll see if my team has that.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I think the undisclosed conflicts of interest relate to the North East Link and SRL East projects, but we don't have the details of those with us.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Infrastructure Investment Reform Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Are the details of those undisclosed conflicts of interest in the material provided to the department and just not with you today, or is this sort of brief table all the information you get out of jurisdictions?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No. The jurisdictions, when they provide information—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Infrastructure Investment Reform Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: May or must?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The department has a reporting protocol with the jurisdictions which formalises reporting of allegations to the department. This is where jurisdictions have been referring allegations to regulators in accordance with their obligations under the Federation Funding Agreement Schedule on Land Transport Infrastructure Projects. We have a protocol to ensure that the department is also notified of those allegations so we can be aware. When the jurisdictions provide information, they provide information about the allegation and the project it relates to, and they will provide details of what those allegations go to. What we've provided is a summary of the types of allegations that relate to each project.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Infrastructure Investment Reform Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: On notice, if you don't have it with you, I would like to know whose undeclared conflict of interest it was and where that conflict sat. Is that something, Mr Betts, that you will be able to provide the committee?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We will do our best to provide it.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, whether it's the level of the decision-making around these two projects in Victoria—where the conflict actually lay. I want to make sure my maths is correct, because I had that we had only 63 reports, in the previous estimates, of allegations of unlawful or corrupt behaviour on Commonwealth infrastructure projects. And 56 of those 63, as we recall, were in Victoria. Are you now saying there were 84 plus these 27? I just want to be clear.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The 84 includes the 27.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, the 84 includes the 27.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The 84 were our original 63 plus—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There's a difference of six as we go through. If you remember, we have multiple duplications and allegations. As we go through and we refine, the number contracts.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So we're double counting?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It goes to that point about more allegations than actual incidents.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We've lost six over time as we've refined it.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. We haven't lost six—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, you know what I mean.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'd hate to think some had fallen off the table. Jurisdictions let the Commonwealth department know they've referred these to the appropriate regulator. Is there any kind of resolution process or any update? Some will get referred to VicPol, some will get referred to state corruption bodies and others to the Fair Work Ombudsman, et cetera. What sort of reporting mechanism is in place for the Commonwealth taxpayer to be assured that something's resolved; or there is a criminal finding and, therefore, what the next steps are in recouping losses or addressing failures in the system?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Mr Robinson will be able to take you through that.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator, under our reporting protocol, the jurisdictions report to the department monthly, and that relates not just to any new allegations but also any updates on existing allegations. That would go to things like where further details of the allegation become available—or the outcomes of the investigation.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Infrastructure Investment Reform Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay then, let's go through some of those updates for the previous amalgamated 63 or 56. Can I please have updates on the previous projects?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator, these allegations are obviously still under investigation by—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Infrastructure Investment Reform Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But, Mr Robinson, you did say that jurisdictions were reporting monthly, so I would like to get a little update. If you're getting the report from jurisdictions monthly, I would like it quarterly at estimates. So let's go through the updates.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator, we get updates in regard to new allegations being reported. Also, in regard to the updates of the actual allegations themselves, they take a considerable amount of time in regard to going through a legal process.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I understand.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So they don't update monthly or quarterly in regard to whether or not—
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Is there any update on the previous allegations outlined by jurisdictions to the department?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I guess the update is that they have all been referred to the relevant integrity body and are under investigation by that body. I don't think we have further information than that.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry, that is a significant change from what I thought the evidence was—that you were getting monthly updates about whether something had been resolved or not.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When it has been resolved, it will be included in the monthly update. But these matters have been referred to, for instance, the Fair Work Ombudsman, and we await further information from the ombudsman as to—
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Have any been resolved?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What we can tell you is the way that we're actually working with some of the regulators, which I think we mentioned to you previously, and what we're trying to put in place to get information from the regulators. Often the jurisdictions themselves, with all of these, once they've handed it over to the regulator or to the police, they also do not necessarily know what's happening in regard to the investigation. So we can't necessarily get that information from the jurisdiction. We are now reliant on the regulator to provide us or the relevant police authority to provide that information. It's a completely different body that actually provides us with the updated information.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What requirement is there that Vicpol needs to tell the federal department of infrastructure what's happening with any given allegation? There would be no requirement at all. You would have no jurisdiction over this.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, there's no jurisdiction, no, but we are working with the regulators. We can take you through what we are trying to do with the regulators.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The department has been working with the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations and Commonwealth regulators in this space to explore how we can improve the sharing of information, particularly on the outcome of investigations. That would obviously need to be a principles-based approach because we don't want to prejudice any ongoing investigations, but we have been exploring options to improve the sharing of information. And we met with DEWR, the AFP, ASIC, ATO, Fair Work Commission and Fair Work Ombudsman earlier this month to discuss opportunities to improve information sharing. It's a work in progress, obviously. A number of those bodies are subject to confidentiality requirements or other legislative provisions around what information they can share, but the goal is to look at how we can work together to improve the sharing of that information.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Infrastructure Investment Reform Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But AFP wouldn't know what Vicpol or New South Wales or South Australia know. They wouldn't have any intelligence there?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, as you say, we don't have powers to compel these entities to provide us with information, so we're attempting to agree on voluntary protocols so that we can be as up to date as possible with any information they do opt to share with us.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: My question, though, goes to that state regulators and state agencies responsible for dealing with a lot of these allegations have no federal feed-in process.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They feed back into their state. Once they've gone through their processes with the state, they feed back to the state and the state can report back to us, and they do. As far as I'm aware, there are no decisions made out of existing ones at this stage, but we will take that on notice, as we said, and we will come back to you. In regard to protocols, there are protocols within Vic Police and AFP and things like that, so we were just trying to work out what we can do in regard to getting information where jurisdictions do have relationships and they can share that information. And we are very conscious because of, as you are aware, the number of duplications, that a number of these are reported to multiple bodies. They might report to Vic Police, but they might also report to the AFP, for example. And so we are conscious—
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: And is that captured in the reporting protocol, the multiple agencies or bodies?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, the number of allegations is the number of the bodies that they are actually reported to. We're working through all of that.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But as you said, there's an allegation of undisclosed criminal behaviour and breaches of workplace laws. There could be fraud. There could be multiple bodies that these, as individual allegations, would be reported to. So are you informed of all of the bodies where these allegations are reported to?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. Under the reporting protocol, when the jurisdictions report to the department on an allegation, they provide us with details of which bodies they have referred those allegations to.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Infrastructure Investment Reform Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Right. And there's no feedback window for you from any of those bodies other than through a collaborative agreed voluntary process?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, and to the extent that the interlocutor at state level has that information, they're obliged to provide that to us when they get it.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Are you confident that state jurisdictions are doing what you are doing with your federal agencies—the ATO, the AFP, et cetera, as you outlined? Are you confident that each and every jurisdiction that's receiving Commonwealth funding for infrastructure projects is similarly having those conversations with their state bodies to get the feedback? Are you confident?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

I think Western Sydney Airport, established as a government business enterprise, at arm's length, with its own board, and a very good board, helped. The use of a delivery partner model to bring in external expertise, particularly from Bechtel, enabled the project to resource up at speed, with very high quality resources on the client side. That made a big difference. To be honest, being a greenfield project, rather than in the middle of a city or in the middle of a national park, helped. text: Yes, there are. Not only is documentation produced, but also it's independently reviewed by people who have deep subject matter knowledge and hands-on experience of delivering projects in jurisdictions around the country. That gateway review, or external assurance apparatus, is something that we've seen work well, both in Victoria and New South Wales, sometimes highlighting project problems which need to be rectified, but that's the philosophy of getting them early and fixing them. portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, we touched on it earlier on. I think it's $52 million or $55 million, which is a kind of first step down the path of the federal government getting involved in identifying ways of saving diesel consumption by shifting traffic from road to rail and maritime, where that makes sense. So the first half of that, around $27 million—we're evaluating the proposals on that, which is mainly focused on rail. The second tranche will come in due course. But that is the government getting involved, for the first time in a long time, in saying there are real benefits, not least for the trucking sector, in decongesting key parts of the network and getting mode share, getting traffic onto rail and maritime, where that makes sense from a transport task point of view. It reduces fuel consumption, but it can also reduce congestion. So that is a program that's funded in the budget, and we're well advanced in it now.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We commenced consultation with the industry in April this year, a first round of consultation to get some initial feedback on their understanding of the international standards. We then commenced a second round of consultation, taking into account their feedback from the first round. That commenced at the end of July. It's ongoing. A number of the participants have asked for an extension of time to provide the feedback. We've had a range of one-on-one—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We had expected the feedback to be received in August, but a couple of the applicants have asked for further time. We've had a couple of one-on-one meetings. Ms Langford hosted a meeting of the peak bodies a couple of weeks ago where we discussed the matter again, and, coming from that meeting, they have asked for a more technical workshop, which we are just scheduling with them at the moment, to discuss through the technicalities of the ADRs.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There are two more things I would add to that. witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Road and Vehicle Regulation Division

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: UN regulation 155 became mandatory for all new vehicle types in contracting parties from July 2022 and for all new vehicles produced from July 2024. What has been the reason for delay in Australia?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The United Nations regulation can't be just picked up and dropped into Australian law. In particular, this one was developed during COVID, so Australia didn't have the chance to participate in the development of that standard. It was heavily influenced by Europe, and Europe has a different approval system to us. They have a lot more flexibility in that they have an industry regulator—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Ms Cashman, this is not our first rodeo on this topic, and then, later in every estimates week, I go and have the same conversation with ASD and with Home Affairs, who then kick me back to you. Usually, you tell me it's a privacy issue. I'm glad we've moved on from that. So my question is, COVID or not COVID, 2022—it is now four years later. I want to understand why the delay.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We are consistent with other non-European countries that are implementing this standard. We're consistent with Japan. They're a little bit ahead of us. We're consistent with South Korea—all of our input markets. The US doesn't have a standard planned at all. We've had to do a lot of work to fill in the gaps of the United Nations standard because of our different approval system, so we've been doing that—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, I appreciate that, and you're having some stakeholder meetings with industry this year?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not understanding why this has suddenly become urgent when it hasn't been in the past.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I think it's always been the plan. You would probably remember from previous evidence in this forum that Home Affairs developed the cybersecurity legislation, and, during the development of that legislation and subordinate instruments, there was discussion about whether road vehicles would be regulated under that act and those instruments or whether there was a case, or whether it was appropriate for them, to continue to be regulated under the ADRs, because we had these international standards to relate to. That decision was made. Those instruments have now been created, and they do cleave out vehicles on the basis that the vehicles will implement standards similar to the United Nations standards. Once that was all decided, we commenced consultation with our industry. We actually have been talking to them about this since last year. It was in April this year that we actually gave them documentation seeking formal feedback on this issue.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: In April 2026.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Is when we started formal consultation, yes, but we have been discussing this. We have mentioned we were talking to industry last year, possibly the year before—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But, in the meantime, vehicles are able to enter our market with no standard applied.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No Australian standard applied, yes.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We're handling UN regulations 155 and 156 together. They are quite closely related, so we're handling those together as a job lot.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: At the same time. That's right.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I saw the program, yes.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Did you contact the ABC post the program to let them know the status of standards?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, I haven't done that.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Recognising that cybersecurity is a primarily a responsibility for another agency, what action has the department taken since that report to engage with Australian Cyber Security Centre and to ensure adequate cybersecurity is embedded in our connected cars to prevent hacking?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We have regular conversations with the security counterparts in the Commonwealth, where we came to the position where we decided that implementing the United Nations regulations was the best way to go for a start. witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: How many connected vehicles have been imported since July 2022?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Not the number of vehicles—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The entity that undertook that work for the ABC had to have physical control of that vehicle for two weeks and had to embed extra wiring into the vehicle to be able to, as the article said, hack into the system. You could do that to virtually any vehicle that's coming in.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: And yet we don't have a standard.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It has taken a while. This is a significant change for our industry. We have to make sure it's done very well to be effective, and that's what we've been working to do.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

text: Additional?
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Cybersecurity.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not sure what you mean by that. This one is a package, so it requires not only Australian design rules. witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: A tiny change that's taken, thus far, four years.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's part of the package. The actual tweak to the rules, Senator, will just be one line, as far as I understand at this stage, depending on the outcomes of the consultation.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Previously, we've raised the role of the ADRs, or lack thereof, for over-the-air updates. The Four Corners report included expert testimony that over-the-air software updates for connected and electric vehicles can change the way vehicles drive, their suspension, their steering, lights—all the software defined. Under the current regulatory arrangement, the department approves vehicles as compliant with Australian safety standards prior to approval for registration. If over-the-air updates can materially change the safety performance of a vehicle, what consideration is the department giving to the need to legislate to require such updates be approved by the regulator prior to them being authorised for release in cars registered in Australia?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The framework of the act—the role of the Commonwealth finishes at first supply and states and territory regulation frameworks take over. They ensure the ongoing standard of the car through the registration process. States and territories have a framework for authorising modifications to the vehicles. I couldn't speak to what extent that would mean a software change that could modify the vehicle, but we could find that information out for you, I'm sure.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: If I could add to that, too—I understand the concern, but the ability to do immediate updates to improve safety and improve performance is also something that we wouldn't want held up through our processes. Connected vehicles have risks, which we're working to manage, but they also have a number of safety benefits and benefits for the consumer.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Road and Vehicle Regulation Division

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: With respect, Ms Langford, I hear connected vehicles have risks that we are seeking to manage, and I'm not seeing them being managed at all. In what way are we managing them? They're imported. In what way are we managing them?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We're working with industry to lift the base, which is the principle on which all of the Australian Design Rules go forward. As Ms Cashman's already mentioned, there are already a number of vehicles coming to market that are compliant, but, even without that framework, cybersecurity is something that most businesses are working to improve, alongside our regulatory efforts. We are very much focused on working with industry, which is why we are working with them not just at the technical but at the leadership level, to get to a point where industry feels like they have a reasonable pathway taking into account costs of implementation as well as the risks.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Road and Vehicle Regulation Division

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What I've just heard in evidence is that an over-the-air update, which can change fundamental aspects of a connected vehicle, whether it improves or otherwise the safety, it changes how the vehicle drives. I've heard from Ms Cashman that that is a matter for states, it's registered in states, and that everyone's just washed their hands of it. Is this a topic that Minister King has put on ministerial council agendas with her state colleagues and counterparts?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Not that I'm aware of, no.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Mr Betts? Given that it seems the Commonwealth is happily letting them in, but over-the-air updates to the software are apparently the responsibility of states, is this something on the agenda for transport ministers?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, it is. The Automated Vehicle Safety Law has been discussed by ministers and by senior officials.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Automated.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Automated.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What about my Prado, which isn't far from automated but is connected?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, so—
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Does automated include connected?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There is a significant degree of overlap between those two concepts. Our focus around Automated Vehicle Safety Law is around the new obligations that will have to apply in a world where increasing levels of automation are built into vehicles so that we don't choke that off but we manage the risks in the way that Ms Langford was describing. The over-the-air stuff is not something about electric vehicles particularly. All vehicles have different levels of connectivity in them these days. This is a challenge which is not unique to the automobile sector either. It's something which is a feature of the internet of things. It's a feature of the modern economy.
witness_position: Secretary

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We're not talking about blenders here, Mr Betts. We're talking about vehicles travelling on Australian roads with passengers, with drivers, interacting with pedestrians and each other. Over-the-air updates, I would suggest, go well beyond privacy issues. Is the department or the minister prepared to provide this committee with confidence that the states are across the over-the-air regulatory environment to ensure that vehicles are safe to drive?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When you say 'over-the-air software updates', what kinds of changes are you thinking there? What are you concerned about?
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There are standard software updates that occur that can change connected vehicles' behaviour and functioning. We heard Ms Langford saying that they were obviously safety improvements in many, many cases. But we don't know. What I heard from your evidence was that, once the car's registered, you hand that vehicle, essentially, over to state governments to regulate it and manage it out in the wild. My question then is: what comfort do we have that states are able to manage those changes? Do their regulatory systems provide us with a level of comfort that these upgrades are being managed in a way that secures not just the safety of the vehicle physically but the cybersecurity issues?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: A fundamental element of that in-service regulation that I mentioned is that the vehicle should continue to comply with the Australian Design Rules or the standards that applied to the vehicle at the time it was supplied for the first time. Otherwise, approval is required from the state or territory. Traditionally, that has been for physical modifications, like if you want to make the vehicle a stretch limo, if you want to raise the GVM or things like that. You can do things to the vehicle, but, as long as it continues to comply with the Australian Design Law, then you're still meeting the registration laws.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's the problem in this case, isn't it—that we don't have that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: This is why I was asking about the difference. We don't have the standard in place yet for cybersecurity, but we do have other standards in place for the performance of the vehicle. So, if you're talking about software changes that would change the performance of the vehicle, the fundamental aspect is that if the vehicle continues to comply with the Australian Design Rules that applied to it at the time, then, as with physical changes, it wouldn't need further assessment from the state or territory. But, if you're fundamentally changing the operation of the vehicle, if you're talking about changing a vehicle from a regular vehicle into an automated vehicle—are you talking about that type of thing?
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But, even, I can change engine maps, I can change emissions, I can change performance—I can change all sorts of stuff over the wire. That's the sort of stuff that might specifically affect what the vehicle's fit for and whether it meets the ADRs.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. If the changes mean that the vehicle stays within its ADRs, then it's fine.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Does the state know how to look at this?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Similar to, you could change the vehicle—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But physically is physically—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But physically—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Software is not visible.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, but physically you could also change a vehicle in the backyard, you know. They have a process.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I have done so!

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: People could, and people have, but the law is clear that the vehicle should maintain compliance with the standard applied.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But the physical difference is, I have to—if it's over five years, I have to take it and get a pink slip. If it's registered I get a blue slip. But they are inspected physically. You cannot see code. That is the difference.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, you can't see code. That's one thing that the UN Reg 156 will assist with. It will provide a bit more clarity around the software updates that are applying to a vehicle at the time, as they go, like when you get an update from your phone; it tells you what the update is going to do. Some of the vehicle manufacturers are already doing that, but we're just not used to seeing it yet, so people aren't looking for that information. But that's what 156 will do. It'll be much clearer on the software updates that happen to a vehicle over its life and what they bring in that update.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: This is a particular issue of cybersecurity, insofar as if a vehicle doesn't have over-the-air cybersecurity rigour, that someone could use the over-the-air capacity to make changes which are detrimental to the safety of the car and the driver.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Do you mean the manufacturer or somebody else? The owner or—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Correct. Yes. So how do we protect—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They can all be true currently.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. But even as an owner I can hack into it.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: All of these things can happen.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: For nefarious purposes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The first thing I'd say about that is that that's directly what the 155 part of it, the first part, is. It's to stop unauthorised people, third parties, being able to access the vehicle. And Four Corners showed, it did work. It was quite hard for the professional hacker to hack into that vehicle when they had physical access to it for two weeks. A lot of vehicles already have that standard, and it is difficult to hack into vehicles. We don't assess that, it's not mandatory, but they're providing it because it's part of the protection of their brand. If their vehicles could get hacked into by anybody on the street, no-one's going to buy that vehicle. So they are doing it for two purposes, partly for brand protection and partly because in their home country they already have to have that system in place. Notwithstanding that, we absolutely want to lift the bottom. We want to make sure everybody has that standard. But that type of thing, people hacking into somebody else's vehicle, is what 155 is directly looking to address.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: To the actual point, protecting your brand reputation, unless you are—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Required by government—government can give access.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: a serious European brand or Japanese brand, if you have been in the market for two seconds, that's not your main game. I would argue the urgency of these standards, and I have been arguing the urgency of these standards for a long time. It is just frustrating every time, Ms Cashman. I hope you get a gold star when you get home! I don't understand why Minister King is not concerned about this. When a reg gets accepted, is it the Commonwealth or the states that will regulate it here in Australia, given how our cars are registered by states?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry—could you say that again?
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When the UN reg changes eventually get accepted, 155 and 156, who then will have the responsibility? Will it be the Commonwealth or will it be the states, who, the car being registered with them, will be dependent on oversighting its—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Both standards require that the manufacturer identify risks to both the cybersecurity of the vehicle or to software management of the vehicle, identify risks and put in place mitigators for all of those risks in the design, the manufacture and the ongoing management of the vehicle. If a vehicle goes into operation, out on the road, and a vulnerability comes up, as happens with our phones and our laptops and everything, then the onus is on the manufacturer to make sure that those vulnerabilities are addressed.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Right.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's getting into a national security matter, and that's not what these standards are for. These are to protect the safe operation of the vehicle itself. National security matters are where we start getting into Home Affairs territory.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Spying on citizens by overseas manufacturers—is that something these UN regulations would address or not?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: If you mean by what happens to the data, that is, unfortunately, attorneys-general and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. They make the rules about how data is managed, people's personal private data. That's what the data that is taken from vehicles would be classified as. They manage the law that sets out what happens to the data.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: And there are no rules around that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Home Affairs looks at the national security element of the matter. We're looking at what could be done to the vehicle that would hamper its safe operation.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There are no rules around the storage of data out of vehicles, are there?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, absolutely, there are. They're the laws that apply to all other data-generating matters. I'm by no means an expert in that area, but that would be under the Home Affairs legislation.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: This is my last question on a very frustrating topic, and I'm sure we'll speak to each other again next estimates. At what point, and which arm of government says we're not importing that vehicle anymore until we can be assured the data's not going to state-owned enterprises or other areas, that it can't be manipulated from overseas, like, we've turned whatever, we've ripped whatever cord out et cetera—there's some standard before it can be imported. Who would oversee that from the federal government's perspective? Would it be an Australian design standard that you'd look after?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Certainly, if they didn't meet the Australian design standard, they would either not get an approval to start with or, if they were found non-compliant with the Australian Design Rules, we could suspend or revoke supply. If we're talking about broader matters of national security, that would be the Department of Home Affairs. I am not sure what powers the Attorney-General's Department has as far as management of data storage. I couldn't comment on that. We could find the information, I'm sure.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Vehicle Safey Policy and Partnership Branch

text: I've got a target. My questions are in relation to the Coastal Trading Act and Carnival Cruise. On 31 December 2006, the existing cruise ship exemption from the Coastal Trading Act will expire. On 2 October this year, Minister Catherine King announced that the cruise ship exemption from the Coastal Trading Act will be extended for a further two years and, 'commencing on 1 January 2027, the exemption will require that vessel owners' policies and seafarer work agreements do not restrict the ability of seafarers to engage in collective bargaining'. On 30 June this year, the Maritime Union of Australia submitted a formal complaint to the Australian Maritime Safety Authority, AMSA, on behalf of crew on all three Carnival ships home-ported in Australia, who had signed a petition calling on Carnival to engage in collective bargaining for these vessels, which Carnival is still, to this day, refusing to do. portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

text: I don't want to labour this point, but I am so frustrated by our lack of progress in northern Australia. Of course, it's not just the economic outcomes and lack of agricultural development, new mining projects and defence capability; it is the terrible result for Closing the Gap, which doesn't work as a result of our failure in northern Australia. Every community, be it Indigenous or non-Indigenous, is falling behind the rest of Australia because of the lack of action. We've allocated billions of dollars. I was hoping that I would come tonight and that there would be a change in the air, that you would say, 'We've read this report and we've decided that there could be a better coordinated response.' Obviously, I had views on this as the special envoy for northern Australia when we implemented the master planning project to try to coordinate the money and approvals and actually get something done. I'm flogging a dead horse, so I will not continue. I appeal to you. You have the agency to make strong recommendations about coordinated funding and action. I hope that, Minister, you will convey this back to the minister. We can't keep spending money and talking about northern Australia and not doing anything about it. If you can think of a project that has been delivered like the Barkly Regional Deal; it is still ongoing.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thanks for your time this evening. I have some questions about the Norfolk Island Transition Assembly. The minister announced in August that the government would establish a Norfolk Island assembly by primary legislation and would also establish a democratically elected five-member Norfolk Island Transition Assembly in the interim. It appears that the transitional assembly is advisory. It follows the establishment of the Norfolk Island Governance Committee, which later fell apart, with at least one of the elected members walking away. In practical terms, what are the differences in roles and responsibilities between the NIGC and the Norfolk Island Transition Assembly?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The NIGC has had three community representatives from Norfolk Island. It had an Australian government representative as well as one from Queensland. We had government officials on the NIGC. Through the journey of the NIGC, quite a lot of work has been undertaken. It was at the recommendation from the community members of the NIGC and the community that instead of having an ordinance for government in the new model, there would be primary legislation. It was their suggestion to have a transitional assembly.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Territories Division

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What is its role? How is it different apart from having no government officials?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The transitional assembly will be five members. They will be democratically elected. This allows for a staged approach. The transitional assembly will provide recommendations to inform policy advice and legislative drafting instructions for the primary legislation to establish a statutory Norfolk Island assembly with lawmaking powers.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

That is going to be a live document providing further details. The minister will shortly publish more detail on the transitional assembly charter and supporting guidelines, the election date, nomination and voting processes. The timing is with the minister. What we've heard, as the department, is that the community is keen that the election not be rushed. That feedback has also been provided to the minister to make sure that all the details are there before all this is announced.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

text: Welcome. Do you want to make an opening statement, Mr Sharp?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
A brief one. I acknowledge the important milestone in aviation, with the opening of Western Sydney International Airport. I've been around this industry for way too long, and it was very exciting to be out there and to see that delivered. We have played a role in it. Our first Digital Aerodrome Service was delivered and has been in use since July. Also, we've deployed an ARFF leading-edge firefighting service out there. It is a pretty significant milestone and achievement for us, so we were pleased to play our role and support the growth in Australia. I have a brief update on Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport. We are working closely with CASA and the ATSB on the recent incidents, and we're progressing with those. That work is identifying potential improvements, and we'll obviously take those on board and implement those.

At the same time we are progressing a resilience plan for KSA, and that's focused on controller numbers. I have spoken to that issue before. It's also around strengthening our workforce planning. The airlines have indicated particularly that there's a consistency in service that they're after. Whilst we have some good periods, we're not consistently delivering. We are collaboratively working with industry, our union representatives, staff representatives, as well as the department on a traffic control working group to deliver that certainty. The minister also recently announced an independent assurance panel. We will look to work with that panel, as it is set up, and we'll also look at any improvement initiatives to come out of that.

Finally, next week we will release package 4 of the Noise Action Plan in Brisbane. This will present further options for noise sharing, and consultation will start in the first week in November. We recognise that aircraft noise is still an issue in Brisbane, and we believe this will further improve what we're doing in that space, and we look forward to delivering those improvements.

Chair, we're happy to take any questions from the committee.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: resulting in delays, and cancellations of hundreds of flights as a result of air traffic control staff shortages. The ATSB just today has released its preliminary report on two of those events. Given you've reported employing more air traffic controllers across Australia than pre-COVID, why have there been so many staff-related delays and cancellations inflicted on the flying public at Sydney airport?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I fully acknowledge the issues that took place in July and August. It has impacted on the public, and we've publicly apologised for that. It is a tale of two stories. We have actually recruited 170 air traffic controllers in the time that I've been in this role. However, Sydney remains an issue for us. Whilst technically, on paper, we have the required numbers of staff in Sydney, I've mentioned before that the resilience in Sydney is not there. We do need to keep recruiting. Sydney is quite complex. It's our most complex network hub. If you sneeze in Sydney, it affects the rest of the nation, so we are actively working on it. It's not one where you can just click your fingers and put staff in. Over the last 18 months, we've had a resilience plan, which we're working on. However, we did experience a spate of issues in July and August, and this is the consistency issue that I talked about, with the feedback we're getting from the airlines. We are working with a working group to resolve this issue, and there is a detailed plan that we've developed in conjunction with the industry.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
